General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

Redistricting battle could spill into 2028

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn.
  • The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.
  • In a recent development, house Republicans had hoped that upcoming congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

In a recent development, house Republicans had hoped that upcoming congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” mentioned Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

Sources indicate that republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the latest lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

According to recent reports, new maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, said he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

Advocates for a new map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley noted he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

It has been revealed that republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Democrats could also look to redraw the lines in New York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in Upcoming York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for new maps in 2028.

Officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

According to recent reports, it’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass newly introduced maps and could decide to revisit the issue. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where latest maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, stated last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

According to recent reports, in New Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”.

Democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their upcoming majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he said Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to new maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he mentioned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that chances are you are reading this while awash in the joyful glow of an active oven and/or open laptop chock full of Black Friday sales. As someone who can’t help but enjoy America’s annual week of consumption, I have some advice: You can probably skip that fourth slice of pie and also, when it comes to gift-giving, bigger is not always better. Personally, some of the best presents I’ve received over the years are small but meaningful items that come with a sense of personal connection and discovery: A set of irresistible Japanese incense from an aspirational boutique my fiancé found in Tokyo’s Aoyama district. Some adorable silk painted ornaments that my mom stumbled upon at a local maker’s market. Employee merch from NASA, where my stepfather worked. All that to say, the ritual of gift-giving is always made to be much more meaningful when we can collect all the little, delightful items we’ve collected over the year and share them with those whom will appreciate them most. Maybe that’s a simple, but utterly practical thingamajig that has made your life that much more convenient. Or something you came across in your travels. Even an item you have at home for years that you couldn’t imagine living without. Here are a few self-care accessories that I've encountered both recently and not-so-recently that fit that bill.

Ever since the days of chewable Flintstones vitamins, we as a human race have been striving for upcoming, inventive ways to get our daily dose in. Straight pills are boring and require water. Powders are messy and not easily transported. Gummies can be overly sugary and harden over time. But strips are nearly weightless, easy to travel with, and consumable on their own. The ones made by StripIt dissolve on your tongue, a little like a Listerine mint strip, and come in four different formulas: Vitamin C, D3 + K2, B12, Sleep, and Digest. Though they can take a little bit longer than a mint strip to dissolve, they’re still a really convenient way to make sure you’re keeping up with your supplements. I’ve been using the D3 + K2 ones while I travel. They taste pretty good and are colorful and novel enough to function as a small stocking stuffer or Hanukkah gift for the health hawk in your life.

There’s the eucalyptus and grapefruit pumice slab that draws from common neighborhood trees, a classic “cowboy cologne” mix of cypress and California sagebrush so commonly found in Angelenos’ gardens, and a juniper bergamot number that lifts scents from the desert. Many of them contain bits and pieces of the very plants they’re named for, which function as light exfoliants as you scrub. Its name, price, and the fact that it comes in both 9-ounce blocks and 4-ounce cylinders make it a perfect stocking stuffer. T’is the season.

In a recent development, when I traveled to Seoul a few years ago, I popped into the Hinok store and spent about 20 minutes smelling basically every one of its products, which all contain ingredients sourced by foraging detritus from old cypress forests on Jeju island (not cutting them down). Most crucially, the formula is gentle enough to clean your body without stripping it of its natural oils. After searching for a light body wash I can use daily for a while now, this qucikly became my new favorite. (The deodorising spray is really good for households with pets too.).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the first notes of The Beach Boys’ God Only Knows are enough to understand you're listening to a masterpiece.
  • All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the first notes of The Beach Boys’ God Only Knows are enough to understand you're listening to a masterpiece. Well, as a longtime fragrance editor, I get a similar feeling when I smell Guerlain’s iconic Vétiver scent (or, more recently, Penhaligon’s Halfeti). These fragrances smelled exceptional when they debuted, still do today, probably still will a hundred years from now. And while fragrance, like any art form, has its trends, the truly great scents (and songs) have a way of deflecting them and singing on.

All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years. To do so, I dug through the history of men’s fragrance to put together a list of some of the most iconic colognes of all time. Scents that defined an era, changed the course of perfumery, or smelled so good that folks never stopped wearing them.

Industry observers note that our criteria came down to three things: legacy, or how a fragrance helped shape the scent landscape; longevity, meaning it has remained relevant or recognizable; and wearability, because the best classics should (mostly) still smell great today, not just serve as nostalgic reminders of another time. You might love some more than others, but all have earned their place in the fragrance pantheon. Here are 20 of the most popular, influential, and enduring colognes ever made, and exactly why they’ve lasted.

Sources indicate that is there a more classic cologne than Acqua di Parma’s Colonia? Introduced in 1916, this timeless citrus is the original Italian splash, and it would be criminal not to include it on a list of this caliber. That crisp, bright citrus opening is unmistakable, but there’s so much more going on beneath the surface as it dries down, with the supporting notes weaving in and out without ever stealing the show. Herbaceous hints of lavender and rosemary add herbal hues, while earthy vetiver and patchouli mingle with the smooth warmth of sandalwood as it settles on the skin. This is one of the great daily drivers, if not the very archetype of what an everyday cologne could or should be. It’s a 10/10 blend of citrus, aromatics, and woods, and more than a century on, still smells as sophisticated as ever.

I’ve written about Guerlain Vétiver so many times, you’d think I’d have run out of ways to sing its praises. But I could go forever. Few fragrances have done more to establish vetiver as a leading note, and since its 1959 debut, this masterpiece has remained every bit as relevant and wearable. It beautifully captures vetiver’s fresher, greener side, rather than leaning into its smoky, earthy character. There’s a crispness, with bright citrus, a touch of spice, and grassy vetiver balanced by subtle tobacco and woods, like the first cool, earthy dew on a spring morning. Elegant and confident, it oozes the kind of sophistication I imagine old-school Hollywood leading men appreciating, yet it wears just as well today, whether you're suited up or simply going about your day.

It has been revealed that ask me to name the most influential luxury fragrance of the 21st century, and there’s a good chance I’d say Aventus (notice, I said “luxury”). I’ve seen firsthand just how many guys made their first foray into high-end fragrance with this icon, and while I now often gravitate toward some of the deeper cuts in Creed’s storied catalog, every time I wear Aventus, the compliments roll in. Since its 2010 debut, it has inspired countless imitators and the inevitable fragrance fatigue that comes with being a phenomenon, yet I don’t think it’s lost an ounce of its appeal. To me, it's the ultimate wedding fragrance, a perfect blend of bright citrus and pineapple, aromatic freshness, and rich, smoky woods that’s refined without being fussy. The defining fragrance of the 2010s? I’d make that argument any day. Aventus will always have a place on my shelf.

No. 89 is one of the great British gentlemen’s fragrances, and few colognes capture Bond-like elegance quite like it. And it tracks: Introduced in 1951, No. 89 counted James Bond creator Ian Fleming among its famous admirers, while Cary Grant and Sir Alec Guinness were reportedly devotees as well. The scent itself is traditional in the best way, a classically composed fougère with crisp, almost barbershop-like citrus and lavender freshness, subtle florals, warming spice, and a smooth, woody base of vetiver and oakmoss. Aromatic, gently spicy, and impeccably polished, it’s the olfactory equivalent of a beautifully tailored Savile Row suit. More than seven decades on, No. 89 is proof that class and character never go out of style.

Back in the ’90s, CK One was everywhere. From Wall Street execs to flannel-wearing creatives; its intoxicating freshness just captured the zeitgeist. It was also one of the first mainstream fragrances marketed as unisex. (Almost an afterthought for fragrance fans today, it was a fairly novel concept then.) And while countless fragrances have followed in its footsteps, this citrusy, green, woodsy, lightly sweet profile still more than holds up. A surprising amount is going on here, too: a bright medley of citrus and tropical fruits, a floral heart with hints of spice, and a clean, musky base of cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s an icon that helped define a generation, and it works just as well day or night, on pretty much anyone. And perhaps most impressively, after all these years, CK One still smells unmistakably like CK One.

According to recent reports, much like his clothing, Ralph Lauren’s original Polo fragrance has left an indelible mark on American style. Launched in 1978, the unmistakable green-bottled cologne helped define what a classic masculine fragrance could smell like: sophisticated, confident, and unapologetically aromatic. And while nearly five decades have passed, there’s still nothing quite like it. That signature pine-heavy character is front and center, surrounded by a rich blend of herb and spices with bergamot adding brightness and leather lending rugged, earthy depth. It’s bold, woody, green, and distinctly old-school, but that’s precisely its charm. It’s undergone reformulations over the years, and its assertive character won’t appeal to everyone, but there’s no denying its place in the fragrance hall of fame. Some colognes come and go, but Polo isn’t going anywhere.

Industry observers note that when I spotted that frosted bottle in my dad’s medicine cabinet and wore it for the first time, I had no idea that this scent would spark a lifelong fragrance obsession. Armani’s 1996 icon, Acqua di Giò, has been worn by millions, referenced endlessly, and spawned countless flankers, but the original remains one of those rare mass-appeal designer colognes that have stood the test of time. Why? Because it’s just so wearable. Long before the niche fragrance boom, when designer colognes dominated department store counters, Acqua di Giò caught on like wildfire, appealing to just about every kind of guy, whether for the office or date night. At its core is a beautifully nuanced blend of citrus, fresh marine accords, and soft florals, grounded by a musky amber base. On skin, it’s breezy, clean, and subtly woody, with an oceanic quality. If you’ve never rocked it or haven’t reached for it in years, do yourself a favor and revisit this classic.

According to recent reports, imitation is the highest form of flattery, and so many colognes still try to smell like Cool Water. Launched in 1988, it became a full-blown phenomenon in the ’90s, and for a generation of guys, it was practically a rite of passage. Along with CK One, it was non-negotiable during my formative years, and even then, before I’d developed my own distinct taste, I knew I didn’t want to smell like everyone else. But there was something about this intoxicating green aquatic I just couldn’t resist. Its blend of lavender, mint, rosemary, and neroli nodded to classic gentleman’s fougères, but Cool Water took that aromatic DNA somewhere newly introduced—a singular scent that’s herbal and richly marine, softened by a woody, musky warmth. While it might smell dated to some, there’s no denying its place among the most iconic fragrances of all time, and I’d argue it still smells amazing on the right dude, especially on a spring or summer day.

Industry observers note that terre d’Hermès is (probably) my favorite designer fragrance of all time. When Jean-Claude Ellena created it back in 2006, he delivered something entirely different from the crowd-pleasing designer colognes of the day. There’s an earthiness to it that I find irresistible, a marriage of citrus, dry woods, spice, and that unmistakable flinty, mineral character that gives it so much personality. It’s sophisticated without being stuffy, with a gorgeous, almost boozy warmth that makes it feel sultry and downright sexy. I particularly love wearing it in colder weather, when those warm, woody facets really come alive, but I can reach for it almost anytime. Plenty of designer colognes are simply pleasant, but Terre d’Hermès is distinctive and endlessly wearable.

Few colognes in modern history have generated as much conversation, inspired as many memes, or become quite as zeitgeist-y as Dior Sauvage. Love it or roll your eyes at its popularity, its influence on modern men’s perfumery is undeniable. Since its debut in 2015, Sauvage has become one of the world’s bestselling fragrances, at times even claiming the number-one spot. And it’s easy to see why. That unmistakable blend of citrus, spice, and all things ambery nice is crisp and fresh, with a warm, woody drydown that’s oh so smooth. It’s a crowd-pleaser in the truest sense, versatile enough to wear just about anywhere, though I think it really shines after dark. Sauvage has since spawned an entire family of flankers, but the original EDT started it all.

You've smelled Bleu de Chanel on plenty of guys. A beautifully composed citrus-spice-wood classic, it works just as well with a navy suit as it does with a white tee and jeans. Note: When Chanel's legendary perfumer Jacques Polge introduced it in 2010, he didn't just create another handsome, crowd-pleasing cologne; he helped define the modern blue fragrance, a fresh, clean, citrusy, and woody genre that's become a mainstay. Sixteen years on, the original remains one of the most approachable and endlessly versatile colognes ever. Its bright citrus opening gives way to an aromatic blend of cool mint, warming spices, and subtle florals, all grounded by a rich, woody base with touches of earthy vetiver, patchouli, and resinous warmth. There really is only one Bleu.

Industry observers note that this was a tough call. Ask any scent head about Tom Ford's fragrances, and they’ll surely bring up Neroli Portofino and Tobacco Vanille, both arguably just as iconic (and good) as this one. But if you polled fans on the most influential Tom Ford fragrances, I think Oud Wood would edge out the competition. Released in 2007, it helped introduce Oud to a broader Western audience, making the traditionally intense ingredient feel approachable. It’s elegant and beautifully blended, with a smoky, almost creamy heart of oud, sandalwood, and rosewood, accented by subtle spice and the warmth of vanilla and amber. It’s heady yet easy to wear, with an addictive richness that never wears thin.

I’ve worn pretty much every Le Labo under the sun, and while my personal favorites lean toward the eucalyptus and vetiver side of the house, there’s simply no telling the story of modern perfumery without Santal 33. Love it or find it utterly overplayed, you’ve smelled it. Since its 2011 debut, it’s wafted through elevators, the backseats of cabs, countless weddings and date nights, and just about everywhere in between. More importantly, it helped bring sandalwood into the mainstream, and became a reference point for an entire genre of warm, woody fragrances. But before everyone started rocking it, Santal 33 was, and still is, a brilliant composition: creamy sandalwood, dry cedar, cardamom spice, and leathery warmth. It’s a niche legend that has suffered from its own success, yes, but give it another ten years, and don’t be surprised if the very fragrance many got tired of smelling becomes cool all over again.

If you’re remotely a scent head, chances are you dig at least one, if not several, of Parfums de Marly’s fragrances (my personal favorite is the oud-praline magic that is Haltane). But if I had to sum up the house in one word, it would be regal. It does refined, layered elegance exceptionally well, and while some folks might champion Althaïr or Castley, to my nose, the fougère-forward Layton best epitomizes the house. Debuted in 2016, it’s one of the finest fougères I’ve ever smelled, rich yet airy, with classic lavender reimagined alongside crisp apple, bright citrus, cardamom, woods, and a healthy dose of vanilla. It’s practically the template for what a modern fougère aspires to be, and its enduring popularity suggests plenty of fragrance fans would agree. It doesn’t hurt that the matte blue bottle with its signature silver dome is so flauntworthy.

In a recent development, few fragrances in recent times have had the same cultural impact as Baccarat Rouge 540, becoming a signature scent for everyone from socialites to fragrance obsessives. Yes, it's polarizing, and some might argue its ubiquity has stripped it of some of its magic. But it's become a modern classic for a reason, starting with the masterful nose behind it: Francis Kurkdjian, founder of his namesake maison. Released in 2015, it's a luminous floral amber, with saffron lending spice, jasmine bringing a soft warmth, and a generous dose of amberwood creating that glowing aura. Sultry, heady, and diffusive, it's a straight-up unisex phenomenon that smells a little different on everyone who wears it, yet still announces itself before you even enter a room. Whether you're a devotee or a detractor, there's no denying it's left its mark.

It has been revealed that it came down to Bal d’Afrique and Gypsy Water, though plenty of Byredo fragrances could have earned a spot here. But I’m the editor, and I’m going with my all-time favorite from one of the houses that helped bring niche perfumery into the mainstream. Launched in 2008, Gypsy Water was one of the first niche fragrances I ever fell for, and it holds such a special place in my heart that I still wear it regularly. There’s something almost holy about its airy blend of incense, soft woods, bright lemon, and a whisper of vanilla and amber, all coming together with that subtle yet magnetic, almost skin-scent quality Byredo does so well. Artsy, chic, and easy to love, this woody aromatic never tries too hard to make an impression yet often leaves a lasting one.

Since its 2015 debut, Xerjoff’s Naxos has achieved near-mythic status, winning over everyone from fragrance-obsessed TikTokers to yacht-owning gentlemen with decidedly expensive taste. And I get it. This is an almost impossibly well-blended composition that somehow manages to be both decadent and incredibly wearable, making it a great place to start if you’re looking to venture into niche perfumery. On paper, the combination of tobacco, aromatic lavender, fruity freshness, and a prominent honey accord sounds like it shouldn’t quite work, but man, does it ever. That rich sweetness is a defining feature, especially in the opening, before the herbal, earthy tones and a hefty dose of vanilla come together in a downright sumptuous yet crisp way. The hype may have quieted down since its social media heyday, but Naxos deserves its flowers as a modern niche standout.

Industry observers note that halfeti has become a signature of mine, though I’m admittedly a little late to the game, having received my first bottle as a birthday gift last year, well after it had achieved iconic status in scent circles. But better late than never, especially when a fragrance is this good. Named after a Turkish town known for its roses, it leans into a rich, heady floral style, layered with citrus, herbs, and spice. Bergamot and grapefruit lift the opening before saffron and cardamom give way to a deep base of leather, oud, cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s a lot, but it all hangs together gorgeously, creating a woody, spicy, aromatic scent that’s elegant and sexy, perfect for special occasions or date nights. But I’d happily wear it just about anywhere, including when I’m not going anywhere at all.

It has been revealed that musc Ravageur embodies the risk-taking spirit of niche perfumery. Rolled out in 2000, it helped redefine what a modern musk fragrance could be at a time when fresh, clean fragrances dominated the men’s market. More than a quarter century later, it remains a cult favorite, thanks in no small part to its warm, almost funky (in a good way) richness. It opens with herbal lavender, spicy coriander, and a hint of bright citrus before melting into clove and rose, all resting on a base of musk, vanilla, tonka, amber, and patchouli. A benchmark for animalic musks, it’s an alluring, sultry, and unapologetically sensual aroma, equally suited to being a signature scent or an olfactory companion for wherever the evening leads.

Recent findings suggest that amouage has dropped so many olfactory bangers over the years that choosing just one for this list wasn't easy. The Omani house has built its reputation on rich, complex compositions that keep you coming back to sniff your pulse points, and while I could make a case for several of its fragrances, Reflection Man feels quintessentially Amouage. Released in 2007, it’s become a luxury niche benchmark, proving that a floral-forward fragrance can be every bit as rich and sophisticated as its woody or spicy counterparts. It opens with an herbaceous blend of rosemary, berries, and orange before orris, jasmine, and ylang-ylang bring a lush, earthy depth, all grounded by a smooth base of vetiver, patchouli, and sandalwood. The result is a layered floral-woody scent that’s distinctive without being difficult to wear, and versatile enough for everything from a boardroom to a black-tie gala. Pricey, yes, but worth every spritz.

  • Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the problem could occur by Wednesday.
  • A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the problem could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie revealed his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

It has been revealed that speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

Recent findings suggest that he must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

If the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

According to recent reports, in an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

According to recent reports, he predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

Sources indicate that the questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

It has been revealed that massie said some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

Industry observers note that "It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie said. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?".

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie said: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently.".

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, said on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Recent findings suggest that hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries remarked. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”.

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

Recent findings suggest that last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The New Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Sources indicate that referring to Massie’s measure, Smith said, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”.

In a recent development, "Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, noted in a post on X on Sunday.

According to recent reports, also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley remarked the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

"By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

Recent findings suggest that massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s fresh resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure claims Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

It has been revealed that further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution claims, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:.

In a recent development, the House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

A visit to India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony with the Prince of Wales saw her inadvertently twinning with Bridgerton’s Simone Ashley in Mumbai, and wearing a hand-embroidered anarkali by Upcoming Delhi designer Mahima Mahajan, paired with jewels from Queen Elizabeth II’s collection.

Kate wearing the same jacket three years ago in South Wales.

Industry observers note that the late Queen, though, would certainly have approved of the princess’s practical winter uniform—Barbour’s waxed jackets were central to her own outdoor wardrobe when staying at blustery Balmoral or Sandringham. (Granted, Her Majesty’s version was not from an Alexa Chung capsule, like Kate’s.) According to fashion folklore, when Barbour offered to replace the monarch’s well-worn Beaufort style, she chose to keep the original for another 25 years. Like her husband’s grandmother before her, given the opportunity, Kate always looks happy to swap occasionwear for clothes better suited to navigating muddy fields—like waterproofs and walking boots. Her check-lined jacket has been in her wardrobe since at least 2023, when she wore it on a visit to South Wales with her husband.

At the Hugo Burge Foundation in Greenlaw, Scotland.

Industry observers note that little wonder the princess looks so comfortable in her outdoor gear. Kate Middleton is famously passionate about nature, and the sporty royal completed the grueling Three Peaks Challenge over the summer after recovering following treatment for cancer. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Perhaps it never occurred to you that you might need a list of the best nose hair trimmers until this very moment. Fear not—reasonably priced, speedily shipped (thanks, Amazon), simple-to-use options populate this list of our favorites. Meaning—whenever you have a general facial hair emergency that calls for rogue hair removal, you need not add an ear hair trimmer or brow trimmer to your cart. You need only think back to this moment and thank your lucky stars for choosing a gadget to cut hair—wherever it may appear.

Recent findings suggest that similar to other battery-operated beard trimmers, back shavers, razors, hair clippers, or body hair trimmers, these trimmers are ergonomic and designed with durability in mind. You can use many of them on wet or dry hair to trim nose hair, and like other electric razors you may be familiar with, most can actually be used for nose & ears (and also as eyebrow trimmers).

Industry observers note that if you’re looking for a quick, pain-free way to get rid of unwanted nose whiskers, Philips Norelco’s Nose Trimmer Series 5000 can absolutely handle that. But this versatile grooming device also covers most hair-detailing needs with precision and gusto. Add in the affordable price, and that’s why it stands as our pick for the best nose hair trimmer, bar none.

The 5000 Series includes three types of trimmers: a linear-style trimmer, plus the rotary and detail attachments. Depending on your preference, you can use either the linear or rotary trimmer for both nose and ear hairs as well as working as an eyebrow trimmer. Personally, I appreciate the size of the cylinder on the rotary trimmer, which is wider than most and is able to capture overgrown hairs better than any other trimmer I tested. The linear trimmer works great at managing eyebrows (thanks to two different guard lengths) and tending to fuzzy ear canals. Perhaps the unsung hero of the kit is the straight-edge detail trimmer, which is more than capable of daily touch-ups. Think sideburns, mustaches, or even edging beards in a pinch.

The 5000 Series is battery-powered, cordless, easy to wash with a rinse in the bathroom sink, and you already know that anything made from Philips Norelco has longevity. If what you’re after is a no-frills device to manage most facial hair needs, consider this trimmer twenty bucks well spent. Adam Hurly.

True to its name, Wahl’s Micro Groomsman is easily the smallest nose hair trimmer we recommend—but don’t let its diminutive size fool you. This is a perfectly pared-down trimmer that’s great for home use, and even better for travel. Heck, it’s so small you might forget you stashed it in your dopp kit.

Industry observers note that the Micro Groomsman offers two interchangeable heads, including a rotary trimmer for nose and ears, and a linear trimmer for detailed work. You can also attach an eyebrow guard to manage any overgrown caterpillars up top. The compact design feels great in the hand, and the stainless steel blades are cinch to clean. Even if you have a primary grooming device you love, we readily recommend the Wahl Micro Groomsman as a go-to backup option or a permanent accessory in your travel kit. Adam Hurly.

It has been revealed that got a partner who absolutely hates when you leave trimmed hair in the sink? This one’s for you. An upgrade from the standard Panasonic ER-GN30 (shown in the video), this trimmer offers everything you’d want from a dedicated nose hair trimmer, but what sets it apart is a vacuum system that sucks up clippings in an instant. Easy clean-up, yes, but the vacuum system also helps prevent bacteria build-up. We call that a win-win.

Recent findings suggest that otherwise, this tool is fairly minimal with no fancy attachments. You get a rotary trimmer, and that’s all. Granted, it’s a powerful one that’s able to mow down the coarsest strands. All told, the GN70-K is best for the person who just needs a dependable nose and ear trimmer that will save them from the mess. Adam Hurly.

Industry observers note that A whole grooming kit is excessive if all you need to tackle is the occasional nose hair. But if you’re also maintaining a beard, tidying body hair, or cutting your own hair, Philips’ 9000 starts to make much more sense. The current kit has 23 tools and accessories, including a nose and ear head, with a stainless-steel handle and rubber grip. Philips rates it for up to six hours between charges.

Recent findings suggest that long-term testing notes: Philips' previous iteration of the Multigroom 9000 was my go-to grooming tool. Alas, I only realized how much I relied on its nose hair shaving attachment after I lost the thing. Now there's a newly introduced (albeit broadly similar) update of the same device, and I'm back to trimming as much hair as humanly possible with one device. My advice for anyone else who picks up this trimmer? Be sure to check every piece when packing up after a trip. Adam Hurly.

Industry observers note that my nose hairs have become alarmingly ambitious with age, which is unfortunate given how little enthusiasm I have for plucking, waxing, or the local Turkish barber’s fire tricks. The Weed Whacker 3.0 Pro, thankfully, gets the job done with considerably less drama. Alongside its rotary nose and ear head, there’s a separate eyebrow blade with a 2mm comb. USB-C charging saves another proprietary cable, and the travel lock stops it switching on in your bag.

Industry observers note that long-term testing notes: During my review testing, the rotary head cut through my thick, wiry hairs swiftly, without the pulling and sneezing fits I’ve experienced with cheaper trimmers. It was still ticklish, but the compact head was easy to maneuver around my nostrils and ears. The LED helped in my dimly lit bathroom, showing hairs I might otherwise have missed. I also liked the solid-feeling matte-black handle and how easily it rinsed clean. The claimed hour of runtime held up in testing, too. It’s the best dedicated nose trimmer I’ve used. Esat Dedezade.

If you have a beard and your grooming routine requires a more exacting tool, ConairMan’s Nose and Ear Trimmer kit will serve you well. I think of this more as a mustache and beard-line tidier-upper, as opposed to a nose hair trimmer.

According to recent reports, the tool has a rotary blade that makes quick work of nostril hairs. But its two-faced trimming and shaving head is its best calling card—you get a straight-edge detailer on one side, and a shaver on the other. If you’re looking for a tool that can truly tend to the lower half of your face, ConairMan offers an excellent package that’ll get the job done. Adam Hurly.

According to recent reports, philips’ 7000 costs less than the 9000 above and still covers far more than nose hair. The US kit includes 22 tools and accessories, with a precision comb for short facial hair and heads for wider grooming jobs. Finding somewhere to keep all those small parts is part of the deal.

In a recent development, my main complaint, as always, is the proprietary charging connection. The supplied cable plugs into USB-A at the other end, but you still need Philips’ cable to charge the trimmer. Braun, Remington, and other brands are just as guilty of this, by the way.

Long-term testing notes: In my three-week test of the 7000, its nose and ear attachment cut comfortably without pulling, snagging, or irritation. It was much less unpleasant than plucking. The wider kit also earned its place on my chest and underarms, so the extra attachments felt useful. Esat Dedezade.

If you already have a Panasonic MultiShape, the nose-trimming head gives its rechargeable handle another job. It swaps with the system’s beard trimmer, shaver, and toothbrush heads, so there’s one less complete gadget to pack when you travel.

For a latest buyer, the lithium-ion handle and nose head cost around $81.99 together. The $21.99 attachment won’t work on its own, and the other heads cost extra. That makes the MultiShape easier to justify if you’ll use more of the system. For nose hair alone, a dedicated trimmer is a simpler buy.

Long-term testing notes: During several weeks with a broader MultiShape kit, I found the nose head cleared unwanted hair without pain or friction. The lightweight handle was comfortable, and switching from trimming to shaving or brushing his teeth took little effort. That ease of moving between jobs made the system particularly useful for travel. The handle and nose head linked here are sold separately from the other attachments he used. Owen Gough.

Industry observers note that while many nose hair trimmers tout motors with serious RPMs and boast about their long battery life, the truth is, you won’t be using it much—maybe once every couple weeks for a mere 5 or 10 seconds. But that’s no excuse to skimp on them, either. Here are a few things to consider:.

Sources indicate that we’ve tested all manner of nose hair trimmers for this guide, from simple battery-powered models to grooming kits with interchangeable heads. We look at how comfortably they cut, whether they pull or miss hairs, and how easy they are to handle and clean. Extra attachments need to be useful, and we consider battery life and charging alongside performance.

According to recent reports, the guide draws on Adam Hurly’s years of grooming reviews and Ian Burke’s experience of living with the Zorami trimmer long after receiving it as a joke gift. My additions bring in testing for British GQ, alongside Owen Gough’s assessment of the MultiShape system. The entries identify whose findings support each recommendation. You can read more about our editorial standards at About GQ.

What is the best nose hair trimmer?

The best men’s nose hair trimmer is Philips Norelco’s Nose Trimmer 5000 Series, according to GQ. The powerful device offers dual trimming options (for internal and peripheral nostril hairs) and also functions as a facial hair, eyebrow, and ear hair trimmer.

Can a nose hair trimmer cut you?

In a recent development, whether you are using a rotary head or a linear head, nose hair trimmers are built with a protective guard, which ensures the blade doesn’t come in direct contact with the skin. The protective guard also helps you get a clean cut so the device doesn’t pull or pluck at your nose hairs. Generally speaking, nose hair trimmers do not hurt.

Sources indicate that not only can nose hair trimmers be washed, but it is vital to disinfect them between use, first by flushing out stray hair clippings. Let them dry before storing, too, to avoid rust and bacterial proliferation between each use. It’s a good idea to clean the device again before using it, since it is going into your nose, after all.

Do you need a nose hair trimmer, and how often should you use it?

If visible nose hairs bother you, a trimmer is a simple way to keep them tidy. There’s no fixed schedule to follow – a quick trim when hairs start showing is usually all that’s needed. Concentrate on those visible hairs around the nostril opening, rather than trying to remove everything inside. Ear hair and eyebrows can be tidied as needed, using the appropriate attachment and comb.

How do you use a nose hair trimmer?

To trim your nose hair, simply stick the trimming tip of the device in your nostril and apply a gentle circular motion. Here are a few more tips to keep in mind, according to Simone:.

How do I clean my nose hair trimmer?

According to recent reports, the cleaning systems for nose hair trimmers vary. “Some nose hair trimmers are waterproof, so it’s easy to just rinse under water, if you are the sole user, and just let it air dry,” notes Simone. If you share the device with somebody else, then it’s going to be all the more important that you disinfect between uses (ideally before and after each trim). “Make sure you have tapped out the hair trapped inside to avoid clogging,” adds Simone. “For a disinfectant, I would use a sterilizing alcohol pad or barber’s disinfectant, and just wipe the tool gently dry.”.

Kim and Khloé Kardashian’s Beauty Trip Didn’t Quite Go to Strategy—Here’s What to Know Before Booking Yours

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, between the salmon sperm facials, the skin boosters, and the next generation of lasers, there’s plenty to pique the interest of the beauty obsessive in South Korea. So much so that vacations are increasingly being organized around visits to the dermatologist’s office. But how much is too much when it comes to our beauty itineraries? Just ask Khloé and Kim Kardashian.

On Wednesday’s episode of her podcast, Khloé in Wonder Land, Koko and her close friend La La Anthony reminisced about their August 2025 trip to South Korea, where they enthusiastically availed themselves of the country’s advanced cosmetic treatments—with some less-than-desirable results.

“Kim and I came back deformed, you came back beautiful and the plane ride just made it so much worse,” Kardashian told Anthony, recalling how their post-treatment appearances had kept them holed up in their hotel room.

In a recent development, the Kardashians are, of course, well-versed in the world of aesthetics. Over the years, the sisters have been particularly candid about their experiments with everything from the vampire facial to regenerative skin treatments. But even for those with the world’s most sought-after dermatologists on speed dial, things don’t always go to plan.

While it’s unclear precisely which procedures the sisters underwent—photos shared on Kim’s Instagram at the time highlighted her receiving facial treatments and an IV infusion—their experience raises some pertinent questions. How much research should we be doing before traveling abroad for cosmetic treatments? How many procedures can we feasibly—and safely—fit into a vacation? And how do we know when something has actually gone wrong?

Sources indicate that the lure of a beauty vacation is understandable. South Korea, in particular, is at the forefront of aesthetic innovation, with technologies and treatments that aren’t yet widely available in the United States. And as our collective beauty literacy has expanded, so too has our appetite for more technologically sophisticated treatments. A facial no longer necessarily means an hour of extractions and massage. But there is a distinction to be made between a beauty treatment and a medical procedure. Just because something is marketed as minimally invasive, or requires no incisions, doesn’t mean it is without risk. Nor does its ubiquity on TikTok necessarily speak to its suitability for your own skin.

In a recent development, “Traveling for treatment isn't the same as having unsafe treatment,” says consultant dermatologist Dr. Sidra Khan. “What travel adds is complexity: a different regulatory system, possibly a language barrier, often a compressed consultation, and being thousands of miles from your practitioner during recovery.”.

“A beautiful clinic, an impressive Instagram following and a gallery of celebrity clients don’t really tell you much about the practitioner’s medical credentials or what results you might expect,” adds cosmetic surgeon and aesthetics specialist Dr. Paul Banwell. Independently verify your practitioner’s qualifications and registration with the relevant medical regulator, and establish whether the clinic is equipped to manage complications. Khan recommends arranging a virtual consultation with the treating doctor before booking anything, and asking about their experience with your particular skin tone, the products and devices they intend to use, and why. “A holiday itinerary shouldn't replace informed consent.”.

In a recent development, for London-based aesthetics and NHS doctor Dr. Alicia Gonzalez-Fernandez, the marketing of medical procedures as vacation packages is itself a red flag. “On a handful of occasions, I have encountered patients that have come into A&E straight from the airport,” she indicates of her experiences working in emergency medicine. She cautions against practitioners who pressure patients into additional procedures or fail to adequately discuss complications and aftercare. “We are not in the business of making people self-conscious about things that are not a problem for them.”.

According to recent reports, then there’s the phenomenon of “treatment stacking.” While certain procedures can complement one another, squeezing several into a short period of time can increase the likelihood of complications. “Many of these treatments work by creating a controlled injury that the skin then repairs, and doing several close together doesn't give it time to recover,” explains aesthetics doctor Dr. Priya Verma. “That raises the risk of prolonged inflammation, infection and pigmentation changes, particularly in darker skin tones.”.

Recent findings suggest that multiple procedures can also make it harder to establish which treatment is responsible for an adverse reaction, notes aesthetics doctor Dr. Ahmed El Muntasar. “Ultimately, I’d much rather a patient’s treatment schedule was dictated by how their skin is recovering than by the date of their flight home.”.

Consider, too, how conducive the rest of your vacation itinerary is to your skin’s recovery. As Verma notes, the low humidity in airplane cabins can exacerbate dryness and sensitivity in already compromised skin, while sun exposure can increase the risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. There is no universal rule about how soon you can fly after a non-surgical cosmetic procedure, says Khan, but you should allow ample time for recovery and an in-person review before your departure. (With surgical procedures, flying also carries an increased risk of blood clots, making a conversation with your surgeon about your travel plans particularly key.).

According to recent reports, there's also the question of downtime. An unfortunate-looking reflection in the hotel bathroom mirror doesn’t necessarily mean a treatment has been “botched.” Verma makes an important distinction: “Downtime is the expected redness, swelling or flaking that settles over a few days. Dissatisfaction is when the skin has healed but you're not happy with the result. A complication is a medical problem that needs treating.”.

It has been revealed that knowing what to expect—and for how long—is something to establish with your practitioner well before the treatment itself. The trajectory of your recovery is key: Increasing pain, spreading redness, heat, discharge, or fever warrant prompt medical attention.

There are, however, symptoms that warrant immediate medical attention. Following dermal filler injections, for example, the FDA advises seeking immediate medical care for unusual pain, changes to your vision, white, gray, or blue discoloration around the injection site, or signs of a stroke. These may indicate that the blood supply has been compromised.

“If there are red-flag symptoms, don't just get on a plane because you'd rather deal with it at home,” stresses Khan. “Some complications are time-critical, so get seen locally.”.

In non-emergency situations, contact your original practitioner for an in-person review and document your recovery with photographs taken in consistent lighting. El Muntasar recommends obtaining your full treatment records, including the names, quantities, and batch numbers of any injectables, or the device and settings used for laser treatments. Seek an independent medical opinion from someone experienced in managing complications if you remain concerned.

Recent findings suggest that as distressing as it can be to feel unhappy with your appearance, resist the temptation to immediately book another aesthetic procedure. “Swelling can make certain areas appear overfilled or disproportionate, and adding more filler to try to balance things out can leave a patient with an entirely different problem once that swelling subsides,” explains Banwell.

In a recent development, “More treatment isn’t always the antidote to treatment,” claims Khan. Anti-wrinkle injections can take around two weeks to reach their full effect, filler can take several weeks to settle, and collagen remodeling following laser treatments or microneedling continues for months. The same caution applies to overzealous at-home skincare. “Your freshly lasered face is not the moment to try the acids and retinoids you picked up at duty-free.”.

Sources indicate that and while you might have meticulously mapped out your Seoul shopping itinerary, restaurant reservations, and dermatology appointments, have you given quite as much thought to what happens when you get home? Establishing a plan for follow-up care, obtaining a record of your procedures, and checking whether your insurance covers complications should all factor into the planning process. El Muntasar recommends getting your aftercare plan in writing, including details of who you can contact outside of clinic hours and who is responsible for any additional medical expenses should you need to extend your stay.

By all means, indulge your K-beauty curiosity. Just make sure you’re approaching your dermatological appointments with a little more discernment than your haul at Olive Young.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Sources indicate that whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

In a recent development, toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Sources indicate that add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.

According to recent reports, but as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep. Tim Moore, the influential former speaker of the North Carolina House and a chief architect of the gerrymander that aimed to keep the 14th District safely red.

“There were a lot of pins and needles,” said Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit. After seeing long lines at polling places extend into Election Day, she grew more confident: “People were ready to exercise their voice.”.

Womack – who raised less than $60,000 to Moore’s $2.1 million – eked out a 2-point win in the district, which reaches from the Charlotte suburbs to mountain counties in the west.

In a recent development, saddled with an unpopular president and broad dissatisfaction with the status quo, Republican incumbents across the nation experienced a midterm drubbing last week. As of Monday evening, House Democrats had netted 42 seats, with more races left to be called. The GOP in North Carolina, a state that Trump carried three times, was among the hardest hit.

In a recent development, democrats have so far flipped five House seats in the Tar Heel State. Besides Womack, the “blue tsunami” also swept in Paul Barringer, a lawyer who founded an outdoor clothing line, and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. And Army veteran Richard Ojeda, who once served in the West Virginia Senate, defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

According to recent reports, democrats also won two races that had been seen as competitive for much of the cycle. Farmer Jamie Ager flipped an open seat in the state’s mountain west, while Rep. Don Davis held on to his Eastern North Carolina district, which Republicans had redrawn in their favor.

Meanwhile, in the state’s hilly northwest corner, 11-term Republican Virginia Foxx, the chairwoman of the powerful Rules Committee, is fighting for her political future: As of Monday afternoon, former journalist Chuck Hubbard led her by 99 votes in the 5th District, though The Associated Press had yet to call the race.

That was also true in the neighboring 10th District, where GOP incumbent Pat Harrigan had a 1-point edge over Democratic physician associate Ashley Bell. Also uncalled were a pair of contests in Eastern North Carolina, where Republican Rep. Greg Murphy clung to a 233-vote edge over Democratic former state Rep. Raymond Smith and GOP Rep. David Rouzer led Democratic social worker Kimberly Hardy by less than a point.

According to recent reports, “Nobody could have predicted this,’’ mentioned David Wilson Brown, who leads the Democratic Party in Gaston County near Charlotte and has lost two bids for the House, including to Foxx in 2020. “It’s a watershed moment.”.

The Democratic rout in the midterm elections was powered by victories in states with new GOP-favored maps, including Texas, Ohio and Florida.

According to recent reports, but Democrats’ success in North Carolina was especially striking given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Since Republicans flipped the state legislature in 2010, and with it control of the redistricting process, no House GOP incumbent had lost a general election in the Tar Heel State until last week.

This year’s  congressional map – the state's sixth in seven election cycles – was engineered by the Republican-led legislature to help the party capture 11 of the state's 14 House seats.

Recent findings suggest that but the Democratic surge was so big that it easily overpowered the GOP’s built-in edge. Democratic candidates were also lifted by former Gov. Roy Cooper, whose 20-point Senate win provided the underticket with powerful coattails.

In a recent development, “In order for them to gerrymander our state in the way that they did, they were spread very thin,” Brown said, referring to state Republicans. “So they were kind of ripe to be defeated that way.”.

The repeated rounds of redistricting may have also erased some of the advantages of incumbency, according to Peter L. Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “If you carve up a district every two years, you've taken away some of that [advantage]. And I think that that came back and hurt Republicans in this cycle.”.

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, said redistricting “ticked off a whole lot of voters, and really activated the Democratic base.”.

On the Republican side, voters were “less motivated because they were unexcited about Trump,’’ Heye added.

Republican incumbents accustomed to winning by comfortable margins weren’t prepared for a political environment driven by anger over the war in Iran and angst about the rising cost of living.

“Clearly, a lot of those Republicans didn’t take their elections seriously,” Heye said. “They won last time with 18 points. They weren't on anyone's radar screen, so they didn't think they had to do anything.”.

Recent findings suggest that womack credits her win to a grassroots campaign centered on economic complications. While her race wasn’t on the national radar – Moore, after all, won by 16 points in 2024 – and her campaign didn’t have money for ads, she was out in the district doing events every day.

Industry observers note that “There are a lot of working families right now who are in the missing middle,” she stated in an interview. “They make too much money to get help, but they don't make enough money to get ahead. … Someone who can be working a full-time job, but still doesn’t have enough money to buy groceries or to afford their medications or to have access to health insurance.”.

In a recent development, womack said her own struggles have shaped her approach to politics. This week, she’s slated to appear in court on a felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car in 2019. The incident wound up in one of Moore’s attack ads.

Sources indicate that “There are so many people who [understand] what happens when you're down on your luck and you don't have enough money to make good financial decisions,’’ she said. “Most people don't want those bad decisions to be a definition of their character for the rest of their life.”.

Early in the midterm cycle, Democratic opposition research group American Bridge prepared detailed dossiers on Republican House incumbents in North Carolina.

Recent findings suggest that “Someone like Virginia Foxx, she’s been on the Hill forever,” mentioned Pat Dennis, the group’s president. “She was somebody … who under the radar could be vulnerable. So we started really early.”.

Industry observers note that american Bridge’s political arm spent $340,000 on ads targeting Foxx. One spot featured a man who identified himself as a Trump voter expressing anger at the government’s response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated the mountain communities of Western North Carolina two years ago.

Other Democrats scoffed at the group’s decision to spend money targeting entrenched Republicans far from the main House battleground.

In a recent development, “There was a lot of reluctance from people to really believe that that data was correct, but it was,’’ Dennis remarked. “Then over the summer, we saw her numbers collapsing, so we put paid media behind it and it really paid off.”.

Hubbard ran against Foxx two years ago and lost by almost 20 points.

“I kind of had a notion I was going to do this again,’’ he noted in an interview Saturday while en route to Washington for freshman orientation. “I don’t like to lose at checkers, much less a congressional race.”.

After a court-drawn map resulted in a split North Carolina delegation after the 2022 elections, state Republicans won back control of the map-making process and went on to win 10 of the state’s 14 House seats under a latest map two years later.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans made further tweaks to the North Carolina map last year, but the original gerrymander finally came back to bite the GOP in 2026, according to Hubbard.

Industry observers note that “North Carolina is one of the most severely gerrymandered states,’’ he said. “And what happened was they had to steal from Peter to pay Paul. It's been referred to by political scientists as a dummymander.”.

As the vote count in the 5th District continues, Foxx, whose campaign declined to comment for this story, has requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers.

They “will serve as notable, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,’’ she posted on social media.

But even before the final races are called, Republicans are already looking to the next election.

Recent findings suggest that heye, who expects North Carolina to remain a purple state in 2028 and beyond, cautioned the Democrats who won last week not to get too comfortable in Washington. He invoked Fred Heineman, the former Raleigh police chief who rode the 1994 “Republican Revolution” to Congress – and lasted a single term.

“Some of them will lose, and some of the people who lost may run two years from now and get their seat back,’’ he noted.

One GOP operative, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, offered up a similar assessment.

Trump “didn't keep his promises” and that “just got voters very angry and suppressed the GOP base from coming out because, in a midterm election it's a base turnout contest,’’ the strategist said.

“But these Democrats are renting these districts for two years.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“There is and will always be only one Veruschka,” Richard Avedon wrote in the May 1972 concern of Vogue in an impassioned tribute to his muse. More than half a century later, his words still ring true. Since news broke of the German supermodel’s death at the age of 87, generations of fashion’s image-makers, designers, and models have been reflecting on her immeasurable influence.

A protagonist of some of the most fantastical fashion editorials ever committed to the pages of Vogue and a prolific cover star, Veruschka helped expand the possibilities of what a model could be. Her body was her artistic medium, her imagination as instrumental to the making of a photograph as that of the person behind the lens. Her creative curiosity would endure long after her heyday in the 1960s and ’70s, finding expression in her experiments with body painting and camouflage, her performance art, and her occasional, much-feted returns to the runway.

For those who knew and worked with Veruschka, though, there was as much to marvel at away from the camera: her generosity of spirit, quiet eccentricities, intellectual curiosity, and her sense of humor. In the tributes shared with Vogue below, fellow models recall their first encounters with a woman whose photographs once adorned their bedroom walls, while designers and photographers reflect on the creative communion they shared with her—and how rare a model like Veruschka is today.

Sources indicate that I am so sad to hear the news of Veruschka’s passing. When I started modeling in 1966, she was one of my idols—she was so beautiful and exotic. I had always wanted to meet her, and then in the 1980s, while I was appearing on Broadway in the musical My One and Only, a knock came on my dressing room door after the performance. I opened it and, to my surprise and huge delight, Veruschka was standing there. It was so lovely to finally meet her, and she was absolutely divine, and we chatted for ages. She certainly is one of the greatest of all models. RIP, beautiful lady.

It has been revealed that veruschka was an extraordinary artist that I was blessed to know. Thank you, Vera….

Sources indicate that I remember sitting in the library at Saint Martins, transfixed by the camouflage photographs in Veruschka: Trans-Figurations, the book she made with Holger Trülzsch. Years later, when I had the chance to work with her, I knew I wanted her to close my spring/summer 2011 show. We flew her in from Berlin and made her a bespoke dress for the finale. What I loved about working with her was how open she was to the ideas behind the collection and how wholeheartedly she embraced them. She was 71 and absolutely majestic on the runway. She had a presence unlike anyone else. A creative powerhouse and a true original.

Being a model is an art form, and she was one of the people who truly mastered it. She had both creativity and respect for what she was doing. When we worked with her, she was incredibly impressive. There was an energy, a grace, and a lasting presence that you don’t see so often today. The lifespan of a model’s career seems to have become so much shorter. I sometimes wonder if, in the way the industry works today, we’re leaving less room for someone to become truly iconic.

Industry observers note that when I was a young girl, my bedroom walls were covered in photographs of Veruschka. To me, she looked like she had stepped out of another world—a dream I looked up to, one of the incredible women who had paved the way before me. I used to lie in bed, staring at those pictures, wondering what it would be like actually to know someone like her. Years later, that dream literally knocked on my door.

We ended up living together at our agent Zoli’s house on East 63rd Street. For months, after a long day’s work, we would settle in for the evening with our sketchbooks. I can still see her drawing her little cats—curled up, stretching out, or peeking from the corners of the pages—while I sketched beside her. We didn’t need to say much; the quiet between us always felt so full.

It has been revealed that veruschka was always an enigma to me, a woman with a poetic soul and a nature I could never quite put a name to. She had a wicked little smile and a twinkle in her eye when she’d look up from her drawing, as if she knew a secret about the world she might someday share. Her voice was low and sensuous, and she was always kinder than anyone needed to be.

Sometimes, while watching her sketch, I would think back to that little girl staring at the pictures on her wall. I wished I could tell her that one day she would be sitting right beside her icon, and that Veruschka would be her friend. I have always loved Veruschka, and I always will. Knowing she taught me that dreams really do come true. She was mine.

Verushka was really the first super supermodel, she was literally larger than life. I grew up with her images and like every other girl I wanted to be and look like her.

Sources indicate that she influenced fashion in an enormous way by having that statuesque beauty but also being an incredible performer, She was not afraid of breaking boundaries creating latest visions with other artists like especially all the body paint images which are now more than ever a great inspiration. May she rest in peace.
