Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare.
  • More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.
  • boneless Fresh York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless Fresh York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; promptly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.).

In a recent development, uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Recent findings suggest that combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#170568. The Body and The Teen Drama Fashion Machine

The Body and The Teen Drama Fashion Machine

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Body, Overcompensating, Off Campus… Just when you thought pop culture had reached peak teen drama, the streaming giants release another slew of bingeable highlights to capture the hearts of Gen Z and Gen Alpha viewers, and upcoming audiences for their sponsors.
  • Taking the lion’s share of views at the moment is The Body, a coming-of-age psychodrama set in a Catholic school, which has quickly made its way into fashion fans’ For You pages.
  • Costumed by Mirren Gordon-Crozier, the series features iconic ‘00s designs, including the Dior Saddle bag, a Louis Vuitton x Takashi Murakami Pochette, a John Galliano-era “J’adore Dior” T-shirt, and various Juicy Couture accessories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Body, Overcompensating, Off Campus… Just when you thought pop culture had reached peak teen drama, the streaming giants release another slew of bingeable highlights to capture the hearts of Gen Z and Gen Alpha viewers, and upcoming audiences for their sponsors.

Taking the lion’s share of views at the moment is The Body, a coming-of-age psychodrama set in a Catholic school, which has quickly made its way into fashion fans’ For You pages. Just this week, the Netflix show has amassed 9.5 million views, marking its second week in the platform’s global top 10. It’s also right now the number one show in 39 countries.

Costumed by Mirren Gordon-Crozier, the series features iconic ‘00s designs, including the Dior Saddle bag, a Louis Vuitton x Takashi Murakami Pochette, a John Galliano-era “J’adore Dior” T-shirt, and various Juicy Couture accessories.

In a recent development, fans have responded online, applauding the depth and details of the costuming. “This is why the Y2K clothing in The Body was so accurate,” reads one TikTok with 106,200 views. Another TikTok splices glamorous scenes from the series, showing big sunglasses, velour tracksuits and flip-flops, soundtracked to Gwen Stefani’s 2004 hit, “Rich Girl” (257,000 views).

Recent findings suggest that “With a show set in 2004, the pieces had to feel real — not like a costume of the era,” says Gordon-Crozier, recalling that a lot was sourced vintage and last-minute finds in local Toronto thrift shops. “The ‘J’adore Dior’, the Juicy, the City bag, and the Murakami were the status language of those girls.” Since the show aired, Gordon-Crozier has received hundreds of messages on Instagram asking where pieces are from, along with compliments on the styling. “Y2K fashion was loud, optimistic and completely unembarrassed,” she says. “It was pre-Instagram, so there was no algorithm telling you what to wear.”.

Industry observers note that true to the period, Gordon-Crozier even recreated tabloid clapback tees, including ‘Team Aniston’ and ‘Team Jolie’ tees for the identical twins Bailey and Britt Bradley. “That generation grew up on latest, flashy pop stars like Britney Spears, Paris Hilton and Christina Aguilera, who were all about excess and fun,” she adds. “Today, there’s so much curation. Quiet luxury I’m sure is a response to that in a way.”.

“Teen dramas have become Gen Z’s lookbook,” states Rick Jackson, marketing agency Pion’s head of B2B content. “Unlike a traditional ad, a show places a product inside a character, and a lifestyle young people already aspire to.” As such, the City bag or the Juicy Couture tracksuit isn’t just shown, but lived, he explains. “Because Gen Z watches with their phone in hand, an outfit can go from screen to TikTok to checkout within hours,” he adds. This is a massive draw for brands, and arguably a far stronger marker of credibility than paid media.

Balenciaga’s City bags were sourced especially for the The Body.

In a recent development, many brands are wise to this already. H&M consistently ties its collections to Netflix youth hits, channeling the mood of each series into capsules: ’80s retro for Stranger Things, romcom prep for To All the Boys and bold retro looks for Sex Education. This consistency is key. Based on Pion’s recent report into Gen Zalpha (16-24-year-olds), cultural relevance needs ongoing presence in youth culture — on screen, through sport, music and movements — instead of a single, one-off moment.

According to recent reports, “Placement gives brands cultural relevance with a generation that’s sceptical of traditional advertising,” states William Weeks, Pion’s chief marketing officer. On the primary market, he explains, interest converts fastest when there’s an accessible entry point. That might mean a discount, a dupe-friendly price point, or a smaller item from the brand. Merch can also fill this gap.

But resale will reap the rewards first, experts agree. Luxury pieces can generate traction as resale offers young fans a way to tap into the moment at a fraction of the price. “For brands, these series are less about a direct ‘buy this exact item’ moment and more about spotting cultural momentum early,” says Sophy Vanner, a strategy partner at creative agency Amplify. “Often, secondary platforms get the first wave of demand because fans want the hunt and the specific reference point.”.

In a recent development, “The smartest brands play both,” says Weeks. “They win the cultural moment on screen and make it affordable for young fans to buy into straight away.”.

Vanner argues that another way primary brands can still win is by leaning into the codes, lore and IRL spaces around those moments: “Turning on-screen energy into real-world hangouts, collabs and shared rituals rather than just another product push.”.

According to recent reports, euphoria has served as the playbook here, offering everything from pop-ups where guests can have their makeup done, DJ-ed events and talks. In 2022, A24 also released a makeup line with Euphoria's makeup artist Donni Davy called Half Magic. Globally, the number of TikTok videos posted using #EuphoriaMakeup increased by 1,051% year on year between November 2025 and October 2026, TikTok shares with Vogue Business.

The Half Magic brand was founded by A24 and Euphoria makeup artist Donni Davy.

Recent findings suggest that in February next year, Amazon will air the second season of Benito Skinner’s Overcompensating, a comedy about a closeted ex-footballer. The show has quickly become known for its very 2010s costumes. Already, the first season (aired in 2025) has built a cult following around its preppy fare. Mall prep brands such as J.Crew, Polo Ralph Lauren, and even L.L.Bean have become associated with the male characters.

“We were trying to tap into archetypal ways that people represent themselves — the way that kids try to fit in by overdressing in the version of the thing that they want to be,” notes the show’s costume designer Hanna Puley. “For the girls it was a lot of fast fashion. I think we pulled a fair bit from H&M and stuff that was readily accessible and felt familiar. It’s that Forever 21 aesthetic.”.

The costuming tracks with a shift that’s been underway for a while among young consumers. Mall brands are having a comeback, accessible luxury is performing (Ralph Lauren revenues climbed 10% in the last quarter), and nostalgic pre-loved designer accessories continue to captivate. It’s exactly why brands should look to these love-triangle, first-kiss dramas to position themselves in the zeitgeist.

It has been revealed that consider also Amazon’s Off Campus, which rolled out in May and follows a men’s ice hockey team in their heterosexual dalliances. Aside from the usual plot analyses that flood TikTok, the show has also built a strong online contingent of fans wanting to discuss the outfits. Leading female protagonist Allie Hayes, played by Mika Abdalla, appeared in one episode wearing a recreation of Jennifer Lopez’s Donatella Versace-designed dress for Halloween. The piece went viral on TikTok, with creators sharing behind-the-scenes footage of costume designer Charlene Akuamoah at work and, of course, their own reactions. One video shared generated 258,200 views.

“I think part of what makes Off Campus resonate so strongly from a fashion perspective is that the clothing strikes a balance between aspiration and relatability,” states Akuamoah. “I was intentional about mixing contemporary brands, vintage pieces, and different price points to create wardrobes that felt authentic to each character. Younger audiences are increasingly turning to television for fashion inspiration, and social media allows them to immediately identify, share and shop what they see on screen.”.

Off Campus star Ella Bright attends the Miu Miu Womenswear Spring/Summer 2027 show.

Across the board, the teen drama genre remains a well for fashion inspiration. Past contenders include US first-love hit, The Summer I Turned Pretty, Spanish private-school thriller Elite and A24’s Euphoria. With them come merch opportunities for the streaming platform and commercial careers for actors beyond the significant screen. A24 is no stranger to merch, and after Euphoria, starring actresses Zendaya and Sydney Sweeney have both gone on to become style icons in their own right, closely followed for their press tour wardrobes and brand ambassadorships with Louis Vuitton and Miu Miu, respectively.

Recent findings suggest that “These demonstrates used to be about putting products on screen, but today the real value sits with the cast themselves,” indicates Alison Bringé, Launchmetrics’s chief marketing officer. She points to the average media impact value (MIV) of an Instagram post from some of The Summer I Turned Pretty’s leading stars: Lola Tung ($387,000), Christopher Briney ($256,000) and Gavin Casalegno ($354,000). “Their fandoms don’t just watch: they follow, recreate and share, which turns these actors into commercial voices with real staying power,” Bringé adds. “That’s why we’re seeing brands sign them as ambassadors rather than treating them as a one-season moment.”.

According to recent reports, similarly, Ella Bright, an Off Campus star, commands an MIV of $757,000 per Instagram post. Selena Gomez’s Rare Beauty also confirmed Bright as its first-ever brand ambassador in July. The news culminated in a MIV of $4.6 million within a week and lifted the brand’s overall performance by over 138% the same day, with the top post driving $815,000 in MIV alone. In September, Belmont Cameli, another star from the series, generated $943,000 in MIV in one week for Saint Laurent through a single post.

It has been revealed that devin Barrett, General Idea’s copy director for social and culture, indicates that teen dramas offer brands a direct link to vibrant cultural conversations and the opportunity to align with future breakout talent. He points to The Body as a fictional portrait of the affluent 2004 teen consumer, explaining that it proffers a upcoming style inspiration source beyond the oversaturated ’00s paparazzi imagery. “Highlights like this bring Gen Z and Gen Alpha into an era they didn’t originally experience, orchestrating a richer world around Y2K aesthetics,” he says. “It unlocks the potential for new brand ambassadors with an authentic connection to products like the Dior Saddle bag.”.

Of course, fashion has long been a fan of teen dramas, both on television and in the movies. Millennials and Gen-Xers might remember Grease, The Breakfast Club and Mean Girls as historic style inspirations. Highlights, however, offer a more enduring marketing avenue for brands to tap into throughout a storyline. “These shows freeze a fleeting, perfect moment — the first love, a friendship group that feels like the whole world,” states Katy Lubin, Lyst’s VP of brand and communications. “The characters are flawed and human. For a brand, being part of that feels genuine in a way a campaign shoot just can’t.” As she sees it, specific pieces become associated with specific character traits, much like the Fendi Baguette gave a cool, New York yuppie association through Sex and the City’s Carrie Bradshaw.

Benito Skinner, director and lead in Overcompensating, attends the Burberry Spring/Summer 2027 show.

Ultimately, because viewers follow highlights for long periods across seasons, it means the fashion choices can also shift and evolve, presenting new opportunities for brands. Competitors will need to be agile. Indeed, next season, Overcompensating is leaning into a different vibe, Puley tells Vogue Business. She’s interested to see how viewers react. “We’re not veering so mainstream. There’s a lot more niche stuff,” she notes.

Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (379 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights.
  • According to recent reports, the seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home.
  • More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

According to recent reports, the seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood is rich in striking, darkly memorable imagery: Margot Robbie shimmying in a sunshine-yellow two-piece at the Playboy Mansion; the sunbaked menace of Brad Pitt’s visit to the Manson ranch; the audaciously bloody denouement, all pit bulls and flamethrowers, playing out high in the Hollywood Hills, with the glittering carpet of nighttime Los Angeles extending endlessly beyond.

Industry observers note that but for some—this writer included—the film’s most indelible legacy is its costumes. And, more specifically, those of Pitt’s laid-back (and possibly wife-murdering) stuntman Cliff Booth. Double-denim layers, gold-rimmed aviators, scuffed moccasins—and, of course, those Hawaiian shirts—the character’s late-’60s California cool burnt up the screen and almost certainly played a part in the Americana wave that plenty of menswear fanatics are still riding.

Industry observers note that so, when David Fincher stepped into the director’s chair for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth—the Netflix film picks up the story of Pitt’s character nearly a decade later—the task of evolving those indelible looks fell to one of the director’s most trusted creative collaborators: costume designer Trish Summerville. Indeed, the trust ran so deep (the pair had previously worked together on The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, Gone Girl, and Mank) that Summerville didn’t even know what the project was when she mentioned yes. “I’m always in for whatever he’s doing,” she tells Vogue. “I don’t know anyone else I would do that with.”.

Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth, Elizabeth Debicki as Karen Crosby, Scott Caan as Charlie Peters, and Carla Gugino as Toni Becka.

Recent findings suggest that across the eight-year gap between the two films, a lot has changed in Hollywood—not least in its style. By the late ’70s, it’s the heady era of Studio 54 excess, punk-rock rebellion, and Halston halter necks. Still, rather than leaning into disco-fever, polyester-everything clichés, Summerville looked to the real-world period artifacts she could get her hands on locally, scouring the vintage mail-order catalogs and archival racks at Los Angeles’s legendary Western Costume, among other places. Under Fincher’s famously exacting eye, every garment had to serve the story without ever feeling like, well, a costume—and it was a challenge that required building nearly every piece from the ground up. (Though with a little inspiration from some select vintage garments along the way.).

Arguably most seductive of all are the costumes worn by Elizabeth Debicki: in Cliff Booth, the six-foot-three Australian actor plays Karen Crosby, an enigmatic, glamorous Hollywood studio executive whose crisp wardrobe practically gleams within the seedy underbelly of 1970s Los Angeles conjured by the film’s production designer, Donald Graham Burt. Dressed exclusively in varying shades of white—a strict mandate from Fincher that required extensive color-testing with cinematographer Eric Messerschmidt—Debicki’s looks deliberately stand out, but never feel disconnected from the world around her.

Recent findings suggest that “Unless it’s something in the script that really wants the clothing and the costumes to jump off the screen, I never want it to distract,” Summerville notes, a sentiment that could apply to the lived-in textures of her costuming work on Cliff Booth as a whole. “It should just help you watch this story.”.

Below, Summerville talks figuring out exactly the right cut of 1970s denim for Pitt, looking to Lauren Hutton and Cher as muses for Debicki, and why the decade’s unstudied sex appeal continues to shape fashion today.

Vogue: Obviously, you’ve worked with David a number of times before—but how did this project end up in your lap?

It has been revealed that trish Summerville: It came up through Ceán Chaffin, who’s Dave’s producer. We met at a coffee shop, which was very formal for us, and she didn’t really say what it was—she just stated that they had a project coming up, a film, and they’d like me to do it, but she couldn’t tell me what it was because it was quite secretive at that time.

Industry observers note that I had to say I was in without knowing what it was. Because of my history with Dave and really liking working with him a lot, I’m always in for whatever he’s doing. I always hope I’m available when he has a project; I hope I’m asked to do it. The only thing I knew was it was a film and it would be in LA, and that was all I knew until I agreed. And then I got an explanation of what it was, and a text from Dave afterwards saying, “Yay, I’m glad you’re in.”.

It has been revealed that I presume you had seen the first film. Did you revisit it before starting work?

Yeah, I definitely had seen the first film, and after they did call me, I did rewatch it so I could get refamiliarized with the characters, but then I got the script, and realized there’s not a lot of overlap in the characters—it’s pretty much just Brad, so it’s a whole new story about him.

When we last saw Cliff Booth, it was 1969, and this film is set 1977. How did you first start thinking about the ways in which his look—and the look of the city generally—was going to feel distinct from the first film?

Industry observers note that I did a lot of research. We have a couple of rental houses here that have pretty extensive research materials, and Western Costume is always a great place to start. They have a search library of periodicals, photographs from sets, behind-the-scenes stuff, and every kind of catalog you could imagine. So it was really important for me to look at everything from films in Hollywood that were happening, behind the scenes, the actors, and then also looking at everyday catalogs like JCPenney or Sears catalogs, looking at Vogue magazine, Ebony magazine—just so I could have a range. It needed to cover what’s depicted on screen as the movie within the movie, then also, how people dressed every day.

According to recent reports, even though there wasn’t fast fashion like there is now, in that amount of time you did see a shift in silhouettes across both men’s and women’s clothing—shapes of jeans, shapes of jackets, the jewelry. But with Brad’s character, it was really about keeping the integrity of who his character is, and the ease—Cliff Booth is really just a fucking cool guy. It was about shifting him a little bit: changing the silhouette of his jeans, giving him Roper suede boots instead of moccasins, not doing as many layers this time, having his shirts buttoned a little bit lower. He’s really, really comfortable with who he is.

Oh, and we definitely wanted to start the film off with the Hawaiian shirt from the first film, so the audience has something to immediately recognize and feel a kinship with.

Tarantino is known for having quite detailed descriptions in his scripts about costumes. Was that the case here?

In a recent development, yeah, in some instances there were. Some of the descriptions of Cliff, it would say he’s wearing Billy Jack boots, or that he puts on puka shells for when he tends bar. But it wasn’t excessive. We stuck pretty much to anything that was a key story point, or that seemed really integral to the character—he’d maybe describe that he’s wearing sunglasses here, or a leather jacket. With Hot Rod, it would describe the style of clothing he would wear, but nothing as specific as a color or anything like that.

How much of the costumes were sourced, recreated, or made from scratch?

It has been revealed that pretty much most of it was made, at least for our principals. When it’s a period film, and you have stunts, and a really long shoot—we shot, I think it was 105 or 107 days—you really have to have at least doubles of things. It’s too scary. We kind of have a saying in the costume world: “If you have one, you have none.” For Elizabeth, we made her costumes, especially because Dave was very specific that he just wanted her always in a tone of white, and white is very scary in general.

Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth and Elizabeth Debicki as Karen Crosby.

It has been revealed that and with Brad’s character, even the shirts that we found for him—like the Hawaiian shirt and the tiki shirts and the liquor bottle shirt—we bought rayon fabric and printed all those ourselves. For the liquor bottle shirt, one of my shoppers found a vintage one and sent me a picture, and I was like, “Oh my God, that shirt is amazing.” Then I found another one, and then one of the guys in our department stated, “Wait, I think I have this shirt at home—I’ve had it for 20 or 30 years.” So we found three different versions of that shirt from the mid-to-late ’40s to the ’70s. I selected all the bottles I liked from the different shirts and changed the colors a bit, and the illustrator I work with drew up a pattern, and then we had a printer here in Los Angeles print up the fabric. We even built jeans for him—we found a Levi’s shape that was great on him, and then we built multiples of them. His barong—the shirt he wears at the end—we ended up making 68 of that particular shirt. It’s all embroidered, all natural fibers, because of how the shirt is used for him and his stunt guy.

Brad knows a lot about fashion—he has his own cashmere line, for one. Was dressing him quite a collaborative process?

Recent findings suggest that it is. He does have opinions, and he’ll bring in inspiration pieces or things that he likes. Then it’s just trying a bunch of shapes, and retrying things once we build them. He really liked the idea of having T-shirts that leaned into an automotive inspiration for Cliff, which makes sense, and we chose to use that at the speedway in the figure-eight races. Working with the Evel Knievel logo, because Evel Knievel was so significant at that time, and being a stuntman, he would really have an affinity for that. And then Brad was like, “Oh, I want a red, white, and blue helmet.” So we went to the props guy and noted, “We’re going to have this Evel Knievel vibe for him for the T-shirts—could you have a helmet painted for him?”.

In a recent development, brad’s great about little details, like keeping on these native beaded bracelets that he wears always, which wears them in and gives them a lot of life. And he took some of the jeans and his bracelets home at the end, which is nice.

Sources indicate that tell me about working with Elizabeth. Was there anyone specific from Hollywood history or otherwise that you were looking to when figuring out her wardrobe?

Recent findings suggest that I was really inspired a lot by Lauren Hutton for Crosby, because you can’t deny that if you saw Crosby, she could be a fashion model. Even though her character is rooted in reality, she’s very glamorous. Lauren Hutton had this really classic look to her, but very sexy, and with this edge—she would wear very drapey tops and really fitted high-waisted pants with silk blouses. There was also a little Cher vibe too, with the drapey halters. And Elizabeth was a lot of fun to dress. She’s really great about exploring character—with her, it was more talking about who Crosby is and what her day-to-day is like. I always try to work very closely with the production designer and the director of photography. Debicki’s going to be wearing white: how white can I be? Can it be optic white? Does it have to be a toned-down white? For some of her costumes, we had to do two different versions for when she was outside versus inside, because the tones read so differently.

Like Brad, Elizabeth looks amazing in those high-waisted trousers and flares.

It has been revealed that she really does. It was so fun. In that figure-eight racing scene when she’s walking through between the bleachers up that little alleyway, it was quite nice to see other people in the cinema take a gasp—because she stands out so much there in this all-white look, so elegant and beautiful. And right before that, when she’s walking down the street at the premiere—so elegant and chic and regal.

Were there any other moments that, when you saw the film on the big screen, you were especially satisfied with?

It’s hard to choose, because I really loved the Manila stills that you see as flash-cut stills—that was several days of shooting, having this whole Filipino vibe, and these brothels, and a Filipino rock band to dress with big platforms and crazy makeup. I also love the scene when Hot Rod is leaving the movie set, and he’s in the velour one-piece Bordeaux jumper with the saddlebags, walking out and talking to Scott Caan. And seeing the tennis scenes—for us, the tennis section was such a big thing because we had to make so many multiples, again all in white, with body-makeup tanner getting on the clothing. And the Verdusco brothers! They would always come together to do their fittings—they never demonstrated up solo—and after we took individual photos, they would always do a back-to-back pose or a karate pose.

As someone who immersed themself so deeply in ’70s fashion for this—an era that’s been cropping up all over the runways recently—what do you think it is about that decade’s aesthetic that remains so aspirational today?

I think it just was cool. People were very sexy without trying to be sexy. You didn’t have to have all your skin exposed—it was something about the silhouette and the drape of the fabrics and the ease. Silk blouses that are just a little bit open, thin gold chains, and the nice drape of the pants. People were so much more carefree then; music was big and fun, and you were out and dancing. I keep joking, “Oh my God, can we please just have jeans with no stretch in them?” Because it’s such a better fit, and the weight of that denim was really nice. Plus you had disco, punk rock, rock and roll: it lent itself to individuality.

Did any of that rub off on your own wardrobe after wrapping the film?

Recent findings suggest that yeah, actually! For the premiere, I wore the jeans worn by Lauren Glazier, who plays Raquel, Brad’s bartending partner. At the speedway, she’s wearing a pair of ’70s Levi’s with a good boot-cut flare to them, and I borrowed those and wore them to the premiere with a Tom Ford dinner jacket. I definitely had to wear six-and-a-half-inch heels to accommodate the length, because she’s quite tall and I’m not!

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the best body trimmers for men are one of the most important grooming tools in your medicine cabinet. Whether you’re looking to trim your down-there hair, corral your pits, deforest your back, shave your ass, or all of the above, it’s good to know your options. And, because dealing with body hair doesn’t always mean shaving it all off, the best body trimmer for you is the one that gives you the results you want.

According to recent reports, you might want a multi-purpose manscaper for hitting all points north, south, east, and chest. You might want a skin-so-smooth shaver that leaves you more hydrodynamic than an Olympic swimmer. You might need something that’s body-part specific. ("Best trimmer for balls" is a perennially popular search for a reason.) The point is: No two men will take the same path on their body hair journey. This is why we’ve done the work, testing every body hair trimmer we can get our hands on, and we've found the best body hair trimmers on the market for just about every guy who needs one.

Sources indicate that black Friday is here, and the deals are hitting fast. For the biggest and swerviest markdowns, editor favorites, and elite-level shopping intel, keep it locked on our roundup of the best Black Friday deals and best Black Friday clothing deals.

According to recent reports, the Philips 7000 is a convincing way to clear some space in the bathroom cabinet. Its bundle pairs body combs for 3mm and 5mm trims with attachments for beard, nose, and ear hair. That gives it a broader role than a dedicated body shaver, particularly if you want to keep some length on your chest.

According to recent reports, my usual Philips complaint applies – it still needs its own charging cable rather than the same USB-C charger that works with your iPhone. Depending on which bundle you pick up, you also might not have an “intimate comb” supplied with it, so I’d choose the Meridian Slimmer for a close trim below the belt.

Recent findings suggest that long-term testing notes: During three weeks with the 7000, it worked through my thick chest hair without pulling. Its slightly boxy handle was surprisingly comfortable around my underarms, with a textured grip that stayed secure at awkward angles. I also liked how well it handled facial hair, giving me a reason to keep one tool handy for several jobs. Esat Dedezade.

According to recent reports, while you might be able to get away with leaving your trimmer at home for a weekend by the shore, things have a way of unraveling fast over longer trips and vacations. For extended stays, you’ll want to pack a handy grooming companion to keep you tuned up from head to toe. The Lawn Mower 5.0 Ultra is designed to cross state lines and beyond: from the handy travel lock to keep the trimmer from powering on in your carry-on to the high-quality travel case to keep its attachments and charging cable organized.

The unique design of two adjustable length trimming guards allows each to be used to achieve three different lengths, which makes for easy transitioning and also saves space in the carry case. In our testing, the trimmer performed with reassuring power and accuracy. While 60 minutes is not the longest battery life, the trimmer’s constant RPM motor ensures the blade won’t slow down as battery levels dip. In any case, when it is time to charge, the Lawn Mower 5.0 Ultra supports USB-C and wireless charging. Adam Hurly.

Sources indicate that if you’re ballin’ on a budget, Remington’s All-in-One Groomer is a capable, familiar trimmer that shouldn’t set off any fraud alerts on your credit card. Out of the box, this lightweight grooming tool is comfortable to hold, and the blade head twists into place with a satisfying click. The trimmer’s three fixed guards offer a standard spread of lengths, ranging from 3–9mm; and, for anything in between or beyond, the adjustable comb guard unlocks 10 additional length settings between 2–20mm. We were particularly impressed by the adjustable guard, which proved to be a handy tool for safely fine-tuning short to medium-length body hair with confidence. With additional attachments including a nose and ear trimmer, as well as a refined detail trimmer, the All-in-One Groomer lives up to its name, providing full-body coverage at an affordable price. Adam Hurly.

Won't settle for anything but the kind of hairless finish worthy of an Olympic swimmer? Philips' Body Groomer 5000 is the device pick up over a conventional trimmer. Its Triple Protect shaving system combines trimming and foil shaving, and there's also a separate trimmer head with adjustable combs covering 1–7mm. So you can leave some length on your chest or switch to the foil for a closer finish.

Industry observers note that that head and comb arrangement differs from the British kit I reviewed, which had fixed guards and you’ll also need Philips’ own charging cable. It’s a familiar gripe when rival devices offer charging over UBS-C, but a small one next to how comfortably the shaving system worked for me.

Long-term testing notes: Over several weeks with the 5000, I used the cutters on either side of the foil to take down longer chest hair, then angled the foil against my skin to clear the stubble. Rushing through dense patches caused the occasional tug, but slowing down solved it. Below the belt, I got a smooth finish without cuts or irritation, and the light handle stayed comfortable through a longer session. All of which left me happy enough to put my wet razor away for a while. Esat Dedezade.

Recent findings suggest that shaving your own back is a time-honored chore for the hairiest among us, and the Mangroomer Intellimax Pro brings a home-inventor level of crazy brilliance to a job that otherwise requires extreme contortions. You just unfold it, power it on, drop it over the first shoulder, and get to mowing. The trimming head doesn’t bite or leave marks, but will take hair down to the normal .5mm, while the foil-head shaver attachment will get you smooth-skinned (for maybe a day or two). You can even adjust the length of the Mangroomer’s handle for taller torsos or to get better angles on tricky spots.

It has been revealed that it was a lifesaver for me when I was single (before I could sweetly ask my partner to do the job)—and so simple that shaving my back almost became fun. I would use it directly in the shower, making for easy cleanup. (Though never with the shower running; it's waterproof, but I didn't want the handle getting slippery enough that I’d drop it.) I never had any issues with nicking or razor burn with the Intellimax Pro’s main trimming head, though it was trickier to get a uniform shave using the foil shaving head. Frankly, it was easier to just use the .5mm trimming head every day if I wanted to stay stubble-free. Adam Hurly.

The Slimmer’s compact head is its main attraction. There’s less machine to maneuver around tight spots, with two combs for leaving some length and a light for a better view – it stays off when you first switch the device on, and another press of the power button brings it into play. USB-C charging also saves you packing another cable. I just wish Meridian had included a pouch – with a trimmer this small and two loose combs, it feels like an obvious omission.

Its two combs cover 1.6mm or 4mm of hair length, so there’s some choice when you don’t want to take everything off. If you prefer longer chest hair, the longer guards on Meridian's Original model make more sense. Still, the Slimmer is the device I’d pick when close control over a blade matters most.

Long-term testing notes: I relied on the Slimmer for around a month on my chest and below the belt. The narrow head made awkward spots easier to navigate, and it cut through thick hair without pulling or nicking me. Without a comb, it left a hint of stubble I was happy with, although the Philips 5000’s foil gets smoother results. As for its ergonomics? The soft, grippy handle was comfortable, and the hinged blade made it easy to rinse out trapped hair. Esat Dedezade.

The OneBlade arrived on the scene years back as a hybrid between an electric trimmer/shaver and a manual razor, with replaceable cartridges ensuring you always had the sharpest cutting surface. The Intimate SkinProtect version steps up the game with coated teeth that protect against bites without compromising on stubble maintenance. For truly sensitive areas, I’d still recommend using the low-profile buffer guard to prevent friction or snips. And if you’re already a OneBlade owner, you can just buy the Intimate SkinProtect cartridges, and swap them on when you start working below the neck.

Right out of the box, the Black Ops inspires confidence with its well-weighted, stainless-steel build—wrapped in a grippy rubber handle to eliminate any chance of a slip. While it may sound like something you’d download for your PS5, the Manscaper Black Ops isn’t playing any games when it comes to getting the job done. The trimmer arrives with eight guards ranging from 1.5–13 millimeters, as well as an adjustable guide comb to give you more options for your hair down there. And, like its amphibious namesake, the Manscaper Black Ops is fully waterproof.

Industry observers note that we look for trimmers that can get through thick growth without pulling and are easy to control when we get to the awkward bits. We pay attention to how securely the guards fit, how comfortably the handle turns around the body, and how much work it takes to get a smooth finish. Cleaning, battery life, and charging matter, too, especially with a tool that may cover several grooming jobs.

Industry observers note that adam Hurly and Dean Stattmann bring their grooming reviews and health and wellness coverage to this guide, For this upgrade, Esat Dedezade has also drawn on his body-groomer testing for British GQ. The entries identify whose findings support each recommendation, and advice from celebrity groomer Dan Perri helps explain what to look for and how to maintain the tools.

What to Look For in a Body Hair Trimmer.

For a professional opinion on what to prioritize when buying an electric shaver or grooming kit, we sought out the expertise of celebrity groomer Dan Perri, who keeps A-list clients like Post Malone, Gerard Butler, and Brendan Fraser looking tidy. Here are the key attributes of a good body hair trimmer, says Perri:.

How do you maintain a body hair trimmer?

“If you want the best performance out of your trimmer, keeping the blade clean and lubricated is key,” says Perri. “Oiling the trimmer every few weeks will keep the blade running smooth, prevent any pulling of the hair, and keep the blade temperature down.” He adds that most trimmers come with a small supply of mineral oil—use it. (Wahl sells a great 4-oz clipper oil for cheap, too.) Be sure to use a machine-safe disinfectant spray to help keep the blade sanitized, which will prevent breakouts, Perri adds.

Can you use a beard trimmer for manscaping?

Some beard trimmers are designed for use on the body, but only if they have attachments designed to keep skin from being pulled into the blade. Keep in mind that the ergonomics of a great beard trimmer doesn’t necessarily align with the ergonomics you’ll want for shaving body parts. You’ll have a harder time hitting hard to reach places, like the back. And beyond that, you’ll want to aggressively sanitize any trimming heads and guards that touch both your face and your… [looks down].

What is the best body hair trimmer for men?

According to recent reports, we recommend the Philips Norelco All-in-One 7000 Series for most people who want to keep some length on their body hair. The 3mm and 5mm body combs let you choose how much to leave. For a smooth finish, go with the Body Groomer 5000 Series and its dedicated foil head.

How often should I trim my body hair?

In a recent development, depends! If you want to be as smooth as an Olympic swimmer, you might want to shave every day. If that's too much of a hassle, doing it every two or three days can be sufficient to have you smooth without your stubble scratching up your shirts.

Should I shave off all of my body hair?

Do you find body hair unsightly? Then maybe you want to shave your body hair to give yourself a smoother appearance. The decision to trim body hair usually depends on what you or even your partner prefers. For professional sports, a hairless body might be preferred for an advantage, like for swimmers or wrestlers.

Is it better to trim body hair when it's wet or dry?

In a recent development, you can shave your hair whether it's wet or dry, but we prefer doing it on dry hair. Trimmers are able to more easily cut through the hair when it's dry, and you can get more even cuts if you're not going for a clean shave. (Though wet/dry trimmers are all over the market.).

What are common manscaping mistakes?

Besides using non-skinsafe grooming electricals (we got you covered in that department), some common manscaping mishaps are the result of poor technique (shaving against the grain), not trimming on cleansed, exfoliated skin, and neglecting post-shaving moisturizing—especially if you have sensitive skin.

Razor burn is no joke. Preparing the skin, using proper shaving technique, and including lotions, moisturizers, and other skin car products into you grooming routine are all good ways to prevent razor burn.

Sources indicate that dan Perri is a celebrity groomer based between NYC, LA, and Florida. His A-list clients include Post Malone, Gerard Butler, and Brendan Fraser.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday.
  • Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.
  • But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the new Congress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the new Congress.

Recent findings suggest that the conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a blueprint to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

Industry observers note that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., noted the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”.

Sources indicate that “I will vote for the delay,” he said. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

It has been revealed that “If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he mentioned, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”.

“People are voicing opinions on all sides of the complications. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”.

Recent findings suggest that no challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators said. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”.

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer said, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., stated voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul stated. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”.

Hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”.

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer remarked.

John M. Donnelly contributed to the report.

  • More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Sources indicate that cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

It has been revealed that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Industry observers note that add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The following article contains minor spoilers for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

Sources indicate that it might seem strange, the notion that people have been surprised to find that a David Fincher film, written by Quentin Tarantino and starring Brad Pitt, is “actually good.” But moviegoers had their fair share of reasons to be skeptical of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth: chief among them, that Tarantino was forcing a mind-melding of the auteurs that could prove disastrously incongruous simply because he didn’t want to blow his long-awaited 10th and final film on a sequel. The 10-film rule is, of course, completely self-imposed, a mandate Tarantino is stubbornly sticking to instead of realizing he can still employ strict curation and quality control without limiting his filmography to a perfect even number. But now that he’s actually, finally, on what will be his last movie (according to his rules), there’s this notion that he’s afraid to pull the trigger—which some believe he all but confirmed when, in 2023, he announced his 10th film would be called The Movie Critic, only to completely retract that a month later.

Two years later, Tarantino sat down as a guest on (what else?) The Church of Tarantino podcast, hosted by two QT superfans, which is actually a pretty fun listen in between all the excessive stanning. So promptly do they bring up QT10 that it’s obvious the director was anxious to set the record straight. Tarantino tells the hosts that TMC started as an exercise in attempting to write a compelling story about “the most boring” profession imaginable. Despite succeeding, he realized he wasn’t excited by it once the film entered pre-production. There was also a version of the story that he adapted into an eight-hour miniseries, until he realized he had no interest in the process of selling and making TV either.

Sources indicate that it’s similar to the way he’s talked about what became Cliff Booth, which started as a novel before morphing into an unwieldy feature script until Pitt convinced him to let someone else take a crack at directing it, lest these titular misadventures go to waste. Watching the film last week, my ears perked up when, in the midst of being courted by Cliff, high-powered Hollywood agent Karen Crosby reveals she got her start in the industry as a… movie critic. She reflects back on her time writing about film derisively, describing the profession as one with a low barrier for entry.

In a recent development, karen is instantly one of the most beguiling characters in a movie filled with colorful performances both big and small. Played by Elizabeth Debicki with an icy, over-it resolve, Karen’s nagging fascination with Cliff makes for what one critic aptly described as Tarantino’s best-written romance since Jackie Brown. Despite being the closest thing to a co-lead, you walk away from the film feeling like you haven’t seen nearly enough of her.

In a recent development, later in the film, Debicki gets a showy, highlight reel-worthy monologue where Karen, instead of extolling the virtues of cinema as a former critic might, recites what’s apparently an infamous credo among her close friends: that film, while entertaining, hardly rises to the level of being true art. (This is much to the delight of one of her clients, A-list TV star Charlie Peters, played by Scott Caan.).

Sources indicate that it was at this point that I was certain we were watching remixed and repurposed scenes from The Movie Critic—and that if Karen Crosby wasn’t the eponymous character, she was at the very least a gender-flipped version. In one of the only times Tarantino talked openly about his erstwhile film, he said it would be “based on a guy who really lived but was never really famous, and he used to write movie reviews for a porno rag.” Meanwhile, the internet ran with the idea that the film would actually be a not-so-thinly-veiled tribute to Pauline Kael. Karen, for what it’s worth, name-drops Kael when describing her past life.

In a recent development, that this is among the best scenes in the otherwise thoroughly enjoyable Further Mis-Adventures only underscores how silly Tarantino’s 10-film imposition is. Look, l I agree with him: as a logline, it hardly sounds exciting enough to be a career finale, but a Tarantino-directed version of the movie probably would’ve been a good time given how much the director clearly enjoys luxuriating in this world. He can write odes to ‘60s and ‘70s cinema in his sleep. But because it would be a retread with no 11th script to follow, it’ll never see the light of day.

It has been revealed that or will it? I hate to enable weird science, but The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth doesn’t simply work; it’s one of the best movies of the year. Can another director submit himself to Tarantino’s tone and vision the way Fincher does so gamely here? Would Fincher even want to do that again? Hard to say on both fronts, but if Tarantino is going to keep being precious about his next (last?) directorial outing, the least he could do is let someone else execute his other ideas before they start collecting dust. Even Tarantino’s B-Tier is still a great time at the movies.
